issues.failure_explanation: The proof only treats the single ordering in which all outliers have the lowest loss, and derives a contradiction by requiring the putative stationary point to lie closer to $\ws$ than the crossing point $\tilde{\w}$. In the vector case this uses the claim that the equal-loss locus of two quadratics $l_i\|\w-\ws\|^2 = l_j\|\w-\w_{b_j}\|^2$ is a halfspace; for $l_i\neq l_j$ it is a sphere (Apollonius), so the halfspace/angle geometry is false. Moreover the target inequality divides $\|\tilde{\w}-\ws\|$ by $\cos\theta_j\le 1$, which enlarges the admissible region and weakens rather than strengthens the contradiction. The remaining orderings (mixed outlier/clean rankings) are dismissed by 'repeat recursively' with no argument, the angle $\theta_{M,\bar{\w}}$ in the hypothesis depends on the unknown stationary point itself, and the radius bound $\|\bar{\w}-\ws\|\le r$ required for membership in $\mathcal{B}_r(\ws)$ is never established. Only the scalar, single-outlier-center, all-outliers-lowest case is actually verified (which reproduces Condition 1).

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For the sake of simplicity, we will assume that $\norm{\nabla f_i(\bs{w})} \leq G ~\forall~i\in \mathbb{O}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The lemma needs a lower bound on $\|\wsgd-\ws\|$, i.e. $\epsilon G \le (1-\epsilon)L\|\wsgd-\ws\|$. The proof derives two upper bounds, $\|\sum_{clean}\nabla f_i\|\le (1-\epsilon)nL\|\wsgd-\ws\|$ and $\|\sum_{O}\nabla f_i\|\le \epsilon n G$, and then asserts an equality with a min; neither yields $\epsilon n G \le (1-\epsilon)nL\|\wsgd-\ws\|$, since $G$ is an upper bound on outlier gradients and outlier gradients may cancel. Counterexample: two outliers placed symmetrically about $\ws$ give $\wsgd=\ws$ while $\epsilon G>0$, so the inequality fails for any $\epsilon'\ge 2/n$ (and is vacuous otherwise).
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: No complete source-supported repair identified; at minimum, a repair must introduce and justify a lower bound on $\|\sum_{i\in\mathbb{O}}\nabla f_i(\wsgd)\|$ (e.g. an alignment/non-cancellation assumption on outlier gradients) and restate Lemma sgdbound and Theorem relativebounds under it.
issues.overall_effect: Theorem relativebounds, whose proof starts from this inequality, and the headline claim that the (worst) MKL-SGD stationary point is provably closer to $\ws$ than SGD's fixed point, are unsupported.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof replaces the MKL-2 outlier weights $2(n-i)/(n(n-1))$ ($i=|\mathcal{G}|+1,\dots,n$) by $1/n$ as an upper bound. This requires $i\ge (n+1)/2$, i.e. $|\mathcal{G}|\ge (n-1)/2$, which contradicts the generality of $|\mathcal{G}|\le n/2$ (e.g. $|\mathcal{G}|=1$ gives weight $\approx 2/n>1/n$ to the top outlier). Furthermore the bracket $f_i(\ws)-f_i(\bs{w_t})$ for outliers has no determined sign, so bounding its coefficient from above does not bound the term; the same unjustified sign assumption underlies the main-text claim $R_t^{(SGD)}>R_t^{(MKL)}$. Hence $R_t^{(MKL_2)}\le R_t^{(SGD)}$ is not established.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restrict to $|\mathcal{G}|$ in the range where all outlier weights are $\le 1/n$ and add a hypothesis controlling the sign of $\eta_t\|\nabla f_i(\bs{w_t})\|^2+2(f_i(\ws)-f_i(\bs{w_t}))$ for outliers (or bound the outlier terms separately), then redo the comparison.
issues.overall_effect: The sufficient condition under which MKL-SGD is 'always better than standard SGD' in expectation (advertised in Section 5) is unproved; the main-text residual comparison claim is likewise unsupported.
